title: Coordinate-axes presentation, total fractions and integral closure
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $b\ge1$ an integer. Write $D=\prod_{i=1}^b k[[t_i]]$ and $R_b=k[[T_1,\ldots,T_b]]/(T_iT_j\mid i\ne j)$, using formal power series [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Let $\rho:D\to k^b$ take constant coefficients, let $\Delta k=\{(c,\ldots,c):c\in k\}$, and let $P=\rho^{-1}(\Delta k)$ with the diagonal $k$-algebra structure. Evaluation on the separate coordinate axes is a $k$-algebra homomorphism $k[[T_1,\ldots,T_b]]\to D$ whose image is $P$ and whose kernel is exactly the ideal generated by the finitely many $T_iT_j$ with $i<j$. It therefore induces $R_b\cong P$. The ring $P$ is reduced Noetherian local with residue field $k$ and maximal ideal $\ker(\rho)$. If $e_i\in D$ denotes the tuple with entry $1$ in coordinate $i$ and $0$ elsewhere, then $D=\sum_i Pe_i$, so $D$ is finite as a $P$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Put $s=(t_1,\ldots,t_b)\in P$. The element $s$ is a non-zero-divisor, $sD\subset P$, and the total ring of fractions (localization at all non-zero-divisors) satisfies
$$Q(P)=P[1/s]=D[1/s]=\prod_i\operatorname{Frac}(k[[t_i]]).$$
Inside this ring the integral closure of $P$ is exactly $D$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. The map $\rho$ induces a $k$-linear isomorphism $D/P\cong k^b/\Delta k$, compatible with the $P$-action through its residue field. Hence $\dim_k(D/P)=b-1$ and the maximal ideal of $P$ annihilates $D/P$.

proof.text: Write $A=k[[T_1,\ldots,T_b]]$. For $F=\sum_Ea_ET^E$, define $\epsilon_i(F)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_{ne_i}t_i^n$. The coefficient product formula in [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] gives $\epsilon_i(FG)_n=\sum_{r+s=n}a_{re_i}b_{se_i}$, because $E+H=ne_i$ forces $E,H$ to be supported on $i$. Thus $\epsilon=(\epsilon_i)_i:A\to D$ is a $k$-algebra map. Its coordinates have common constant $a_0$, so it lands in $P$. For $(f_i)_i\in P$ with common constant $c$, the series $c+\sum_i\sum_{n\ge1}[t_i^n]f_i\,T_i^n$ maps to $(f_i)_i$. Hence its image is exactly $P$.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: Put $I=(T_iT_j\mid i<j)$. Each generator maps to zero. Conversely, if $F\in\ker\epsilon$, then $a_0=0$ (there is an axis since $b\ge1$) and $a_{ne_i}=0$ for $n\ge1$. Every remaining exponent $E$ has at least two positive coordinates. Assign $E$ to the lexicographically first pair $(i,j)$ with $i<j$ and $E_i,E_j>0$. Define $G_{ij}$ coefficientwise: its coefficient at $H$ is $a_{H+e_i+e_j}$ if $H+e_i+e_j$ was assigned to $(i,j)$, and zero otherwise. The product formula of [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] now gives $F=\sum_{i<j}T_iT_jG_{ij}$ coefficient by coefficient. This is a finite sum of genuine series, not a claim about a closed ideal. Thus $\ker\epsilon=I$. The assignments $[F]\mapsto\epsilon(F)$ and $\epsilon(F)\mapsto[F]$ are well-defined inverse $k$-algebra maps $A/I\cong P$. The ideals generated using $i\ne j$ and $i<j$ agree by commutativity. Here the quotient algebra and its canonical map are those of [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient].

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: A field is Noetherian: an ideal containing a nonzero $a$ contains $a^{-1}a=1$, so its ideals are $(0)$ and $(1)$ [def-weil-field, def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. By [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-noetherian], $A$ is Noetherian (there are finitely many variables). For an ideal $J\subset A/I$, its inverse image in $A$ has finitely many ideal generators, and their images generate $J$. Therefore $A/I$, and hence $P$, is Noetherian. By [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-domain] with coefficient field $k$ and one variable, every $k[[t_i]]$ is a domain. If $p^n=0$ in $P\subset D$, then $p_i^n=0$ in each such domain, so $p_i=0$ for every $i$ and $p=0$. Hence $P$ is reduced.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: The map $\lambda:P\to k$ taking the common constant is surjective and has kernel $\mathfrak m=\ker\rho\subset P$. If $p\in P$ has common constant $c\ne0$, each $p_i$ has a power-series inverse by [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-local-ring] with $A=k,d=1$. Taking constants in $p_ip_i^{-1}=1$ gives constant $c^{-1}$ for every inverse, so $(p_i^{-1})_i\in P$ and $p$ is a unit in $P$. Conversely a tuple with common constant zero cannot be a unit since $\lambda(1)=1\ne0$. Thus all elements outside $\mathfrak m$ are units; every proper ideal is contained in $\mathfrak m$, while $P/\mathfrak m\cong k$ by $[p]\mapsto\lambda(p)$. This proves locality, the maximal ideal and the residue field.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: For $d=(d_i)_i\in D$ and each $i$, let $p^{(i)}\in P$ have $i$th coordinate $d_i$ and every other coordinate the constant series $d_i(0)$. Then $d=\sum_i p^{(i)}e_i$, proving $D=\sum_i Pe_i$ and finiteness as a $P$-module by [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. The tuple $s=(t_i)_i$ belongs to $P$. Multiplication by $s$ on $D$ is injective, since the coordinate rings are domains by [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-domain] and $t_i\ne0$. It is therefore injective on $P$. Every $sd$ has all constant coefficients zero, so $sD\subset P$.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: Every nonzero $f=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nt_i^n\in k[[t_i]]$ has a least index $r$ with $a_r\ne0$. Shifting coefficients gives $f=t_i^r v$ with $v(0)=a_r\ne0$, and $v$ is a unit by [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-local-ring]. Consequently every fraction $f/g$ in $K_i=\operatorname{Frac}(k[[t_i]])$ can be written $h/t_i^r$ with $h\in k[[t_i]]$: factor the nonzero denominator $g=t_i^r v$ and put $h=fv^{-1}$. Thus $k[[t_i]][1/t_i]=K_i$. For a tuple of such fractions, take $N$ at least all the finitely many denominator exponents; then its $i$th coordinate is $h_i t_i^{N-r_i}/t_i^N$. Hence $D[1/s]=\prod_i K_i$, as subrings of that product.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: The inclusions in $\prod_iK_i$ identify $P[1/s]$ and $D[1/s]$: indeed $d/s^n=(sd)/s^{n+1}$ and $sd\in P$ by step 5. A tuple $u\in P$ is a non-zero-divisor exactly when all $u_i\ne0$. If all are nonzero, $up=0$ forces $p_i=0$ in every coordinate domain [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-domain]. If $u_i=0$, the nonzero tuple $t_ie_i\in P$ is killed by $u$. Every non-zero-divisor therefore has coordinatewise inverse in $\prod_iK_i=P[1/s]$. Map a fraction $p/u\in Q(P)$ to $(p_i/u_i)_i$. This is well-defined and injective: cross-multiplication in all coordinate fields is equivalent to $pu^{\prime}=p^{\prime}u$ in $P$, since denominators are non-zero-divisors. It is surjective because $P[1/s]$ already equals the product, and powers of $s$ are allowed denominators. This proves all the asserted equalities of fraction rings.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: For $d=(d_i)_i\in D$, write $d_i=\sum_{n\ge0}a_{in}t_i^n$ and put $q^{(i)}=(\sum_{n\ge0}a_{in}t_j^n)_{j=1}^b$. All coordinates of $q^{(i)}$ have constant $a_{i0}$, so $q^{(i)}\in P$. The polynomial $\prod_{i=1}^b(X-q^{(i)})\in P[X]$ is monic of positive degree $b$. At $d$, its $j$th coordinate vanishes because the factor with $i=j$ is $d_j-d_j=0$. Thus it vanishes in $D\subset Q(P)$, proving that every $d\in D$ is integral over $P$ by [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure]. This supplies integrality explicitly rather than invoking a finite-algebra integrality theorem.

source.place: Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross), equal-constant subring and the paragraph following the equation; explicit coefficient and fraction calculations supplied by Q90.

proof.text: The field $k$ is a Noetherian normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]: its ideals were checked in step 3, it has no zero divisors by multiplying by inverses, and its fraction field is $k$ itself, so every element of $\operatorname{Frac}(k)=k$ integral over $k$ lies in $k$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-power-series-normal-domain] to $R=k$. It states precisely that each $k[[t_i]]$ is an integral domain and every root in its fraction field of a monic polynomial over $k[[t_i]]$ belongs to $k[[t_i]]$. If $z=(z_i)_i\in Q(P)=\prod_iK_i$ is integral over $P$, project its monic equation to coordinate $i$. This is a monic equation over $k[[t_i]]$, so that node gives $z_i\in k[[t_i]]$ for every $i$. Hence $z\in D$. Together with step 8, the integral closure of $P$ in $Q(P)$ is exactly $D$.

source.place: Tag 0BI0 (lemma-power-series-over-Noetherian-normal-domain), applied to R=k; coordinatewise application to the normalization assertion of curves.tex Tag 0C1U (equation-multicross).

proof.text: The $k$-linear map $D/P\to k^b/\Delta k$, $d+P\mapsto\rho(d)+\Delta k$, is well-defined. Its kernel is zero by $P=\rho^{-1}(\Delta k)$, and it is onto by choosing the tuple of constant series for any vector in $k^b$. For $p\in P$, $d\in D$, the constant coefficient product rule gives $\rho(pd)=\lambda(p)\rho(d)$, so this isomorphism respects the $P$-action through $\lambda$. Explicitly $k^b/\Delta k\to k^{b-1}$ sends $[c_1,\ldots,c_b]$ to $(c_2-c_1,\ldots,c_b-c_1)$, with inverse $(a_2,\ldots,a_b)\mapsto[0,a_2,\ldots,a_b]$. The usual coordinate vectors give a basis of the latter space, so $\dim_k(D/P)=b-1$. If $p\in\mathfrak m$, then $\lambda(p)=0$, proving $\mathfrak m(D/P)=0$. For $b=1$ these maps are the unique maps of zero spaces.
